summary: Landfall is a project designed to retrieve and leverage NASA data, presented in a casual format while incorporating elements relevant to professional applications. It features over 10,000 locations that users can explore, allowing them to examine data across various scientific parameters. The interface is intended for searching and comparing potential sites for lunar and Martian bases, as well as identifying Earth-based locations that serve as analogues for various types of research and training.
details:
Landfall: Where to land. Where to train.

What does it do and how does it work?

Landfall is a web app that links two questions that are usually answered separately: where to land on the Moon or Mars, and where on Earth to train for that specific site. It runs in the browser with nothing to install, on both desktop and mobile.

The journey has four steps:

  1. Plan the mission. The user picks a destination (Moon or Mars), a purpose (permanent habitable base, mining and ISRU resources, scientific research, continuous solar power or logistics outpost), crew size and duration.
    • Terrain: slope from LOLA (Moon) or MOLA (Mars).
    • Ice: hydrogen from Lunar Prospector, or water-equivalent hydrogen from Mars Odyssey GRS.
    • Thermal: day-night temperature swing from Diviner (Moon) or thermal inertia from TES (Mars).
    • Resources: iron oxide from Lunar Prospector or iron from GRS.

How the engine works. It first brings both terrains to a common resolution, without inventing precision the data does not have. It then removes each window’s reference plane, because the Martian areoid and Earth’s geoid cannot be compared in absolute terms. From there it computes relative elevation, slope, roughness and curvature. The distributions of these variables are compared with statistical distances (Wasserstein-1, Kolmogorov-Smirnov and energy distance), along with the spatial structure of the terrain (variogram and Moran’s index of slopes). Each distance becomes a percentile within the Earth catalog, and candidates are ranked in a way that is consistent with Pareto dominance. There are no made-up weights, no machine learning and no “similarity percentages.” Results are stated in a way anyone can check. For Jezero Crater, for example, the top candidate is “closer than 94.3% of all places on Earth on every measure.”

What are the benefits?

  • From expert judgment to a measurable comparison. Today, analogs are mostly chosen by experience and tradition. Landfall offers a quantitative, reproducible and explained comparison, made for each landing site rather than for “Mars in general.”
  • It finds new candidates. The engine scans all of Earth’s land and can surface places nobody had proposed, which may be more accessible or a closer match.
  • It helps with practical planning: what time of year to go, what the site looks like in the latest satellite image, and what can be trained there.
  • Everything in one journey, from the mission to the training site. It serves mission planners, scientists, educators and the general public.
  • Transparency. Every number shows where it comes from and whether it is measured data or an estimate.

What impact do we intend?

We want every crew to be able to rehearse on the ground most similar to the one they will walk on. Training at a site chosen with data, and not only by habit, can make analog campaigns more useful and help decide where to spend time and money. Landfall is also meant to support analog programs and the teams preparing Artemis missions or future missions to Mars.

It is also an outreach tool. It turns NASA science data, which is usually only accessible to specialists, into something anyone can explore and understand. The methodology is documented and open, so other teams can verify it and extend it, for example with higher-resolution elevation models.

What tools, languages, hardware and software did we use?

  • Web: HTML, CSS and JavaScript with ES modules and no build step. We used Three.js (WebGL) for the globes and the Saturn V simulation, and wrote our own charts in JavaScript.
    • PDS: LOLA, Diviner, Lunar Prospector and LROC for the Moon; MOLA, TES, Mars Odyssey GRS and the Neutron Spectrometer, and the Viking MDIM 2.1 mosaic for Mars.
    • Earthdata / LP DAAC: SRTMGL30 and SRTMSWBD.
    • Live from the browser: CMR (HLS Landsat/Sentinel-2, ASTER GDEM, MODIS), GIBS and NASA POWER.
    • Visuals: Blue Marble, VIIRS Black Marble night lights, real VIIRS clouds from NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 on specific dates, and the Deep Star Maps from NASA’s Scientific Visualization Studio.
  • Video: automated screen recording of the app with Playwright and Chromium, editing and sound effects with Python and ffmpeg, and an AI voice-over made with ElevenLabs.
  • Development: VS Code, Git and GitHub, and Claude Code (Anthropic) as an AI coding assistant. The app is hosted on Render under the domain topgit.earth.
  • Hardware: our own laptops (Apple Silicon Macs). The app picks 8K or 4K textures depending on the device’s power, so it also works on phones.

How is our project creative?

  • It joins two problems into one story. On the same screen, the globe flies from Mars to Earth and the landing site leads straight to the training site.
  • It finds matches without a “black box.” Instead of a score with arbitrary weights or an AI model, the engine uses percentiles and Pareto dominance. Every result can be explained and checked.
  • It makes the data visual: the moon/mars, shows the data with its data layers (iron, hydrogen, temperature, elevation) peeling away one by one, and the two terrains compared side by side at the same scale.
  • Realistic detail: a Saturn V built entirely in code with its stages and separations (with “TOP GIT” where the original read “UNITED STATES”), and real satellite clouds that cast shadows on Earth.

What factors did our team consider?

  • Honesty with data. We use only official sources, and every value is labeled as measured or estimated. If the layers fail to load, the app says so with “DEMO DATA.” At the Martian poles, where the Odyssey GRS team did not publish data, approximate values are shown with “≈” and never enter the scores. We also keep a source registry that records how each source was verified.
    • Each source has a different resolution.
    • Each planet uses a different height reference.
    • In SRTM the sea is 0 m, the same as land at sea level, which is why we apply the water mask.
    • Neighboring terrain cells are not independent, so we correct the sample size.
  • Saying what we don’t claim. The engine compares the shape of the terrain, not geology, rocks, atmosphere or gravity, and the app explains this.
  • NASA’s real constraints for crewed landing sites on Mars.
  • A general audience. The interface is in English and uses plain language. Technical details sit behind “Learn more,” and credits for every source are always visible.
  • Performance and accessibility: textures adapted to the device, a mobile layout and announcements for screen readers.
